status_summary: The economic impact analysis (EPA-452/R-26-002, dated January 2026) for EPA's final combustion turbine standards (rule published 2026-01-15) states that EPA is no longer monetizing benefits from reducing fine particulate matter and ozone, will continue to quantify emission reductions, and will reconsider monetization once it is confident in the modeling. This goes beyond the document's call to identify co-benefits separately, since ozone and fine particulate effects are the main health endpoints of a NOx rule. EPA told the Associated Press that not monetizing does not mean valuing health impacts at zero, while environmental groups called the change unlawful. A second EPA air rule, the final repeal of 2024 Mercury and Air Toxics Standards amendments published 2026-02-24 (91 FR 9088), reports cost savings and no monetized benefits in its Federal Register text; a Greenberg Traurig analysis of 2026-06-24 states that its Regulatory Impact Analysis declines to monetize health benefits and that EPA now gives less weight to benefits from pollutants outside a rule's statutory target, and reports petitions for review of the repeal filed in the D.C. Circuit on 2026-03-30 and 2026-03-31. No rule on consistent and transparent consideration of costs was found, and no legal challenge specific to the change was found.

timeline.event: EPA released the combustion turbine economic impact analysis (EPA-452/R-26-002), which states that EPA is no longer monetizing PM2.5 and ozone benefits (release day per Harvard's tracker; the document is dated January 2026).
EPA published the final combustion turbine rule whose analysis applied the approach.

EPA published the final repeal of 2024 amendments to the Mercury and Air Toxics Standards (91 FR 9088, FR Doc. 2026-03638, effective 2026-04-27); the Federal Register text reports annualized cost savings of 69 to 78 million dollars and presents no monetized benefits estimate.

title: Change cost-benefit practice: focus on targeted pollutant, set aside co-benefits
uncertainties: The release date of 2026-01-12 for the analysis comes from a Harvard tracker; the document itself is dated January 2026 only. The Federal Register final rule (Doc. 2026-00677) was not re-read in this review. The application to the MATS repeal rests partly on a law-firm analysis: the Federal Register text of the repeal was read and shows cost savings, cost-effectiveness and residual risk discussion without a monetized benefits estimate or an explicit statement on monetization, and the Regulatory Impact Analysis was not opened, so the treatment of PM2.5 there is not confirmed from a primary document. The D.C. Circuit petitions (Air Alliance Houston v. EPA, filed 2026-03-30, and State of Illinois v. EPA, filed 2026-03-31, consolidated, as reported by the same law firm) challenge the MATS repeal, not the monetization practice as such, and were not checked on a court docket. Searches through 2026-11-02 found no EPA rule or guidance codifying consistent consideration of costs, and no litigation specific to the monetization change itself.
